review.notes: Built on the course: modes and filters, in-transit cost formula, TEU, FCL vs LCL, revenue ton, air chargeable weight (/6,000), bill of lading types, document consistency, Incoterms risk points, savings method, load planning. Calculations checked. Fictional companies.

content.company: Southwind Trading (fictional), importing appliances and spare parts and delivering to shops
content.briefing: You run inbound freight and local deliveries. This month: a big appliance order from Asia, urgent spare parts, a new supplier contract, and a delivery route that keeps running late. Costs and lead times are on the line.

variants.text: 500 washing machines from Asia: heavy, low value per kg, needed in 8 weeks. Which mode?

choices.f: Lowest cost per tonne. The 8-week window allows it.
Heavy, low value-density goods by air would cost more than the margin.

choices.t: Road from the nearest port only
choices.f: Road cannot cross the ocean. Sea first, then road.

variants.text: 20 kg of spare parts, a stopped production line, needed in 3 days from Europe. Which mode?

choices.f: Urgent and high value: speed is worth the cost.
Weeks at sea while the line stays stopped.

choices.t: Wait to combine with the next order
choices.f: Downtime costs far more than air freight.

variants.text: A shipment worth USD 73,000 sits 30 days in transit. Annual carrying rate is 20%. What is the in-transit inventory cost?

choices.f: Correct: 73,000 x 0.20 x 30 / 365. Add it to the freight rate before comparing modes.
That is a full year of carrying cost. Scale by transit days / 365.
You multiplied by 30 without dividing by 365.

variants.text: Sea is USD 1,500 cheaper than air, but adds 25 days of transit on goods worth USD 146,000 at a 20% carrying rate. Is sea still cheaper?

choices.t: No: about USD 2,000 of extra stock cost outweighs it
choices.f: Correct: 146,000 x 0.20 x 25 / 365 = 2,000, more than the USD 1,500 freight saving.

choices.t: Yes: sea still saves USD 1,500 on the freight bill
choices.f: Freight is only part of it. Goods in transit tie up cash: about USD 2,000 here.

choices.t: Yes: time in transit has no real cost to us
choices.f: Goods on the water are paid for but cannot be sold. That costs money.

variants.text: How many TEU is one 40-foot container?

choices.f: Correct. A 20-foot container is 1 TEU.
That is a 20-foot container.
TEU is twenty-foot equivalent: 40 feet is 2.

variants.text: You need chilled dairy shipped by sea. Which container?

choices.f: Temperature controlled for perishable goods.
No temperature control. The dairy spoils.
Open top is for tall cargo loaded from above.

variants.text: Your LCL cargo is 3.2 cubic metres and weighs 1,800 kg. How many revenue tons are charged?

choices.f: Correct: 1 RT = 1 m³ or 1,000 kg, whichever is greater. 3.2 m³ beats 1.8 t.
That uses weight, but volume is greater.
You added both. Only the greater one is charged.

variants.text: An air box is 100 x 80 x 60 cm and weighs 50 kg. Volumetric divisor 6,000. What is the chargeable weight?

choices.f: Correct: 480,000 / 6,000 = 80 kg volumetric, greater than 50 kg actual.
That is actual weight. Light, bulky boxes are charged on volume.
You added both. The greater of the two is charged.

variants.text: Your order fills only a third of a container. Speed matters less than cost. FCL or LCL?

choices.f: You pay for your space only. Expect more handling time.
Safer and faster, but you pay for two thirds empty.

choices.t: Wait until you can fill it
choices.f: Delaying stock risks stock-outs.

variants.text: A full container of fragile glassware is ready. FCL or LCL?

choices.f: Your cargo alone, sealed at origin. Fewer touches, fewer breaks.
For a full load, FCL is usually cheaper too.
A full container by air is very costly.

variants.text: The bill of lading says 'three cartons damaged'. What type is it?

choices.f: Banks often refuse claused bills under letters of credit.
Clean means no remarks about damage.
A waybill is a different document, not a title.

variants.text: You need fast release at the port and the goods are already paid. Which document fits?

choices.f: Not a document of title, so no original paper is needed to release.
Works, but originals must travel and can delay release.
That proves origin, not carriage or release.

variants.text: The invoice shows 1,000 units; the packing list shows 980. What do you do before shipment?

choices.f: Inconsistent documents cause customs delays and fines.
Customs holds the cargo. Demurrage starts.

choices.t: A sea waybill, not a bill
choices.f: Altering a supplier's document is not allowed.

variants.text: Your new contract says 'FOB Shanghai'. Where does risk pass to you?

choices.t: When goods are on board the ship in Shanghai
choices.f: Correct. You arrange and pay the main freight and insurance.

choices.t: When goods arrive at your warehouse
choices.f: That would be a D rule, such as DAP.

choices.t: When goods leave the supplier's factory
choices.f: That would be EXW or FCA at the factory.

variants.text: Under CIF Luanda, who carries the risk during the sea voyage?

choices.t: The buyer: risk passes at origin
choices.f: C rules: seller pays main carriage, but risk passes when loaded at origin.
The seller pays freight to Luanda, but risk has already passed.
Incoterms set risk between buyer and seller.

variants.text: How should the Incoterm be written in the contract?

choices.f: Example: FCA supplier's warehouse, full address, Incoterms 2020.
Without a named place, risk and cost points are unclear.
A country is too vague. Name the exact place.

variants.text: Depot to shop A: 30 km. Depot to shop B: 40 km. A to B: 15 km. What is the saving from serving both on one route?

choices.f: Correct: 30 + 40 - 15. Pairs with the largest savings are joined first.
That forgets to subtract the A-B leg.
That is the A-B distance, not the saving.

variants.text: The delivery route runs late daily. Drops are in random order and trucks hit city traffic at 8:00.

choices.t: Group by zone and sequence to avoid peaks
choices.f: On-time delivery rises from 70% to 92%.

choices.t: Add a second truck to the same route
choices.f: More cost; the bad sequence remains.
Unsafe, and traffic still wins.

variants.text: A truck has 6 drops. How do you load it?

choices.t: Last drop first, first drop last
choices.f: Each stop's goods are at the door when needed.

choices.t: First drop first, at the back
choices.f: Drivers unload everything at each stop.
Time is lost searching at every stop.

variants.text: A load has heavy drums and light cartons. How do you place them?

choices.f: Stable load, safe braking, no crushed cartons.

choices.t: Heavy on top to hold cartons
choices.f: Unstable and crushes cartons.
Poor weight balance and risk at opening.
